title: Weekly Deep Dive: United Just Told You Loyalty Doesn't Pay What It Used To
summary: United Airlines just raised MileagePlus status requirements by as much as 45.5% while quietly stripping out benefits — and it's not alone. Ryan and Hope dig into the forty-year history of frequent flyer programs, the billions airlines now make selling miles to banks, and why the entire industry seems to be betting, all at once, that you're too loyal to leave.

topic.topic: United Airlines fundamentally restructures MileagePlus elite status, raising requirements by up to 45.5% while devaluing benefits—signaling a potential industry-wide shift in how airlines monetize frequent flyer programs.
topic.why: This story appeared in at least 8 separate articles across major aviation outlets and represents a watershed moment for airline loyalty programs. United's aggressive devaluation—combined with CEO Scott Kirby's candid admissions about monetizing every touchpoint—reveals the strategic direction of the entire industry. Airlines are betting customers are too locked-in to leave, but this gamble will determine whether loyalty programs remain a retention tool or become pure profit centers.
key_facts: United raised MileagePlus status requirements up to 45.5% while simultaneously cutting benefits like free checked bags and lounge access
Status now requires segments flown rather than miles, making it harder for premium cabin passengers to qualify
Southwest's companion pass became significantly harder to earn in its simultaneous loyalty overhaul, suggesting industry-wide tightening
CEO Scott Kirby defended paid upgrades, seat fees, and aggressive monetization in a candid interview, signaling confidence customers won't flee
Multiple competitors (Southwest, American, Delta) are running similar elite tier restructures, indicating coordinated industry strategy
